title: Claws, beaks and teeth grown by unequal permanent accretion are logarithmic spirals

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Claws, beaks and teeth grown by unequal permanent accretion are logarithmic spirals

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Wherever a structure grows by permanent increments with unequal longitudinal growth about its axis, as in nails, claws, beaks and teeth, it always tends to the form of a logarithmic spiral, which becomes conspicuous only when the structure is long.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: unequal longitudinal growth by permanent increments \Rightarrow r = a e^{\theta\cot\alpha}

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The logarithmic spiral _always_ tends to manifest itself in such structures as these, though it usually only attracts our attention in elongated structures, where (that is to say) the radius vector has described a considerable angle.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XIII, “The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion”; topic “Teeth, beak and claw”. Scope: nails, claws, beaks, incisors, canines and tusks of vertebrates

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: unequal longitudinal growth by permanent increments \Rightarrow r = a e^{\theta\cot\alpha}

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch13-13: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.78

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Logarithmic curvature is straightforward to test against explicit alternatives. Large public morphology collections make a strong cross-structure test feasible, although complete universality cannot be demonstrated.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit logarithmic, circular, polynomial and other spiral models to standardized centerlines of claws, beaks and ever-growing teeth across taxa, stratified by structure length. The claim requires logarithmic fits to predominate and become clearer with angular extent; systematic rival superiority refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The universal word 'always' requires broad sampling.

Wear can substantially alter tooth and claw trajectories.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Skull archives already contain hundreds of beaks and teeth whose centerlines can be fit with standard curves, which is enough to test the tendency in those structures. The claim also covers nails, claws, and tusks, which are much less completely digitized, and it says the spiral is inconspicuous precisely when the arc is too short to identify. Existing scans can therefore accept or reject the law for elongated dental and rostral structures and only sketch it for the rest.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit logarithmic spirals and alternative curves to centerlines of claws, beaks, incisors, canines, and tusks, and test whether fit improves as the structure subtends a larger angle. The tendency is supported if long structures converge on a constant spiral angle and short ones are the same curve seen over a small arc; consistently better fits by non-logarithmic curves in long structures would refute the universal tendency.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Nails and claws are rarely CT-scanned compared with beaks and teeth.

Over a short arc, a logarithmic spiral, a circle, and a gentle bend are difficult to tell apart.

analysis feasibility: 0.7
